intro: The finale of La Mer, ‘Dialogue du vent et de la mer’, opens with low strings playing beneath timpani and bass drum. Calls from the first movement return, and a brass chorale sounds in the final fast passage, which ends in D♭ major.

sections.label: A · Low strings and muted trumpet call
sections.mNote: Low strings accompany a phrase on muted trumpet

sections.label: B · Wind phrases over running strings
sections.mNote: Long wind phrases stretch above the quick accompaniment

sections.label: C · Flutes, harps and strings
sections.mNote: Wind solos and harp figures enter between the larger exchanges.

sections.label: D · Brass above the moving strings
sections.mNote: Horns and trumpets enlarge the phrases.

sections.label: Coda · Brass chorale and D♭-major close
sections.mNote: The brass chorale returns before the D♭-major ending.

cues.title: Opening of movement III, low instruments
cues.text: Animé et tumultueux — animated and tumultuous. Timpani and bass drum roll softly while cellos and basses climb in short, twisting figures, and the tam-tam sounds. Most of the orchestra is still silent.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, movement III, printed p. 223: timpani, bass drum, tam-tam and low-string figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Muted trumpet, low strings
cues.text: A muted trumpet plays above the low strings, beside phrases for oboe and clarinet. For part of this passage the double basses bow close to the bridge, which gives their held notes a thin, grainy edge.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, rehearsal 43, printed p. 224: trumpet marked Sourdines; divided basses marked Sur le chevalet.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pierre Lalo’s review, 1905
cues.text: Reviewing the 1905 première in Le Temps, Pierre Lalo, formerly an admirer of Debussy, wrote: “I do not hear, I do not see, I do not smell the sea.”
cues.evidence: Pierre Lalo, Le Temps, review following the Paris première of 15 October 1905, quoted in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy), Reception. Debussy’s reply is discussed at https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer.

cues.title: Wind theme over duplets and triplets
cues.text: In the finale, the wind play a sustained theme in long phrases over much quicker string figures. Beneath it, groups of two and three notes are superimposed.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg describes the finale’s superimposed duplets and triplets and sustained wind theme: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. Durand full score, movement III.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Returns from the first movement
cues.text: The trumpet call of the first movement also belongs to the finale. Debussy brings back its shape among the stormier exchanges and later restores the broad chorale.
cues.evidence: Susan Key discusses the finale’s returns from movement I: https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer. Durand full score, movements I and III; this is a movement-wide relationship.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Flutes and oboes above two harps
cues.text: In the middle pages, the flutes and oboes exchange short phrases above the two harps. The horns hold long notes and the first violins sustain a high line over the moving inner strings.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 250–252: wind phrases, two moving harp parts, sustained horns and first violins.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy conducts La Mer, Paris, 1908
cues.text: On 19 and 26 January 1908 Debussy conducted La Mer himself with the Paris orchestra. The work had met resistance in 1905, and these performances brought him his greatest public success since Pelléas et Mélisande.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note, on Debussy’s Paris performances of 19 and 26 January 1908: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: Return of the brass chorale
cues.text: The brass chorale from the first movement returns in the closing pages. Horns and trombones hold the broad line against repeated wind notes and short string figures. At Très animé the orchestra moves into the final fast section.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 270–274, the chorale and rehearsal 61, Très animé. The established coda boundary locates this closing span.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chords in D♭ major
cues.text: After the orchestra’s last sustained chord in D♭ major, the timpani strike once more with the strings playing pizzicato. Debussy marks this final attack sec — dry.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, final page, printed p. 279: final timpani and pizzicato string attack marked sec. Jacob Greenberg describes the same ending: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Brass exchanges give way to harps
transitions.from: B · Wind phrases over running strings
transitions.how: The brass exchanges die away into a passage for quieter winds and strings. Flutes and oboes share the tune above the two harps, and horns and double basses hold long notes. The first violins sustain high notes above quicker figures in the violas and cellos.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 248–252, the retreat and ensuing harp-and-wind passage.

transitions.title: Brass chorale into Très animé
transitions.from: D · Brass above the moving strings
transitions.to: Coda · Brass chorale and D♭-major close
transitions.how: The key signature returns to five flats and the harmony moves towards D♭ major as the closing brass chorale enters. The chorale’s long notes are held over short, repeated string figures and sustained low brass. A crescendo leads to Très animé, where the strings take up continuous running notes for the final section.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 270–274: return to the five-flat signature, brass chorale and rehearsal 61, Très animé.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement III, printed pp. 223–279: low strings and percussion at Animé et tumultueux, muted trumpet at rehearsal 43, the late brass chorale and Très animé at rehearsal 61.

timeline.note: Timpani, bass drum and tam-tam sound beneath the low strings.
Muted trumpet and woodwinds cut across the low strings; the basses play close to the bridge.
The wind phrases extend across the running string figures.
Flutes and oboes play above the two harps, with held horns and high violin notes.
The brass join the wind phrases while the strings keep up their quick accompaniment.
Short wind calls sound over quick string figures before the orchestra plays the closing chorale.
Winds, brass and strings play the final D♭-major chords; timpani and plucked strings play the last dry stroke.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
